pages.spec: Describe what artificial intelligence is, and what it is not
pages.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is computer systems doing tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognising faces, understanding speech or making predictions. Today's AI is clever at specific tasks, but it does not think, feel or understand like a person.

diagram.title: Film AI vs real AI
diagram.caption: What the films show compared with what AI really does today.

states.label: AI in films
points: Thinks and feels like a person
Has its own goals and plans

states.label: AI in real life
points: Spots patterns in data and makes predictions
Has no feelings or wishes of its own
Very good at one kind of task
Usually software on a phone, laptop or server

blocks.text: Your phone unlocks when it sees your face. Your music app seems to know which song you want next. Your email quietly moves junk into a spam folder. None of these were programmed line by line for *your* face, *your* taste or *that* email. They use **[[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]]**, usually shortened to **AI**.
So what is AI?
**Artificial intelligence** is the name for computer systems that can do tasks that would normally need human intelligence. These tasks include:

items: **Recognising** things: faces, voices, handwriting, objects in a photo.
**Understanding and producing language**: answering questions, translating, summarising.
**Making predictions**: what you might buy, how long a journey will take, whether it will rain.
**Making decisions**: which move to play in a chess game, which route to drive.

blocks.text: Like any program, AI follows an **[[Algorithm|algorithm]]** (a set of step-by-step instructions). The big difference is *where the rules come from*. In a normal program a person writes every rule. In most modern AI, the computer works out its own rules by spotting **patterns** in huge amounts of **[[Data|data]]**.

head: Traditional program
AI system (machine learning)
rows: Who makes the rules?
A programmer writes every rule
The computer learns rules from examples
Example
A calculator: 2 + 2 always gives 4
Face unlock: learns what your face looks like
New situations
Only does exactly what it was told
Can make a good guess about things it has not seen before
Can it be wrong?
Only if the programmer made a mistake
Yes: its guesses are based on probability, so it can be wrong

blocks.text: What AI is NOT
Films are full of robots that think, feel and want to take over the world. Real AI is very different. It is worth being clear about what AI is *not*:

items: **Not alive or conscious.** AI does not have feelings, wishes or opinions, even if it writes as though it does.
**Not magic.** It is maths and statistics running on very powerful computers.
**Not always a robot.** Most AI is software running on phones, laptops and servers. Many robots in factories have no AI at all.
**Not always right.** AI makes mistakes, sometimes very confidently.

blocks.text: A chatbot that says *"I feel happy to help!"* is producing words that fit the conversation. It does **not** actually feel happy. Do not mistake fluent language for real understanding.

blocks.title: Worked example: AI or not AI?
blocks.context: Which of these use AI? (a) A school bell that rings at 8:50 every morning. (b) A phone camera that blurs the background behind your face. (c) A calculator app.
steps: (a) A timer follows one fixed rule written by a person: **not AI**.
(b) The camera has to recognise which pixels are *you* and which are background, in any photo, in any light: **AI**.
(c) A calculator follows exact maths rules programmed by a person: **not AI**.
blocks.answer: Only (b) uses AI, because it has to recognise something in new, unpredictable situations.

blocks.title: Key points
items: AI = computer systems doing tasks that normally need human intelligence.
Most modern AI learns patterns from data instead of following rules written by a person.
AI recognises, predicts, decides and produces language.
AI is not alive, not conscious and not always right.
Most AI is software, not a robot.

check.why: AI is about doing tasks like recognising, predicting and understanding language.

check.q: Which of these is most likely to use AI?
check.why: Face unlock has to recognise your face in new situations.

check.q: Where do the rules in most modern AI come from?
o: They are typed in by the user every time
The computer learns them from patterns in data
There are no rules at all
check.why: Modern AI learns its rules from examples.

check.q: A chatbot writes "I'm so excited!" What does this tell you?
o: The words fit the conversation, but it does not feel anything
check.why: AI produces words that fit; it has no feelings.

practice.q: What is meant by **artificial intelligence**?
practice.a: Computer systems/programs (1) that can perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, e.g. recognising faces, understanding speech, making predictions (1).

practice.a: In a traditional program a programmer writes every rule (1); in machine learning the computer learns its own rules/patterns from data/examples (1). OR: a traditional program only does exactly what it is told (1) whereas AI can make a guess about new situations it has not seen before (1).

practice.a: Any two: not alive/conscious/has no feelings (1); not magic, it is maths/statistics (1); not always a robot (1); not always right (1).

pages.spec: Outline key moments in the history of AI, from Alan Turing to today's chatbots
pages.summary: AI ideas go back to Alan Turing, who proposed the Turing test in 1950. Milestones include the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, Deep Blue beating Kasparov at chess in 1997, AlphaGo beating Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, and chatbots becoming widely used from late 2022.

diagram.title: A short history of AI
diagram.caption: Click each event to read more.

items.label: 1950: the Turing test
items.detail: Alan Turing asks "Can machines think?" and proposes the imitation game.

items.label: 1956: AI gets its name
items.detail: Scientists meet at Dartmouth College, USA; the term artificial intelligence is used.

items.label: 1966: ELIZA
items.detail: An early chatbot that followed simple rules but seemed to understand people.

items.label: 1997: Deep Blue
items.detail: IBM's chess computer beats world champion Garry Kasparov.

items.label: 2016: AlphaGo
items.detail: DeepMind's AI beats Lee Sedol at Go by 4 games to 1.

items.label: Late 2022: chatbots for everyone
items.detail: AI chatbots that write fluent text become free and widely used.

blocks.text: AI can feel brand new, but people have been working on it for over 70 years. The story starts with a British mathematician who also helped to win the Second World War.
Alan Turing and the Turing test

**Alan Turing** (1912 to 1954) was a mathematician who worked at **Bletchley Park** during the Second World War, helping to break secret German codes. He is often called the father of computer science.

In **1950** he wrote a famous paper that asked: *"Can machines think?"* Because "thinking" is so hard to define, he suggested a game instead, which he called the *imitation game*. Today it is known as the **[[Turing test]]**.

blocks.title: How the Turing test works
blocks.context: A human judge has typed conversations with two hidden partners: one is a person and one is a computer. The judge cannot see or hear them.
steps: The judge types questions to both partners.
Both partners type back their answers.
The judge has to decide which partner is the computer.
If the judge cannot reliably tell them apart, the computer is said to have **passed** the test.
blocks.answer: The test checks whether a machine's conversation can pass as human. It does not prove the machine really understands or thinks.

blocks.text: Many experts now say the Turing test is not a good measure of intelligence. Modern chatbots can often fool people in short conversations, yet they still make basic mistakes and do not understand the world the way you do.
Key milestones

head: Year
Milestone
Why it mattered
rows: Turing's paper and the Turing test
Asked the big question: can machines think?
Dartmouth workshop, USA
The term **artificial intelligence** was used for this meeting of scientists (coined by John McCarthy). AI became a field of study.
ELIZA
One of the first **[[chatbots|Chatbot]]**. It followed simple rules to reply like a counsellor, but some users believed it understood them.
Deep Blue beats Garry Kasparov
IBM's chess computer beat the world chess champion in a six-game match.
Voice assistants on phones
Talking to your phone became normal for millions of people.
AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol
DeepMind's AI beat one of the world's best players at **Go**, a game far more complex than chess, by 4 games to 1.
AlphaFold
DeepMind's AI predicted the 3D shapes of proteins, helping medical research. Its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Late 2022 onwards
AI chatbots go mainstream
Free chatbots that write fluent text were used by millions of people within weeks.

head: Deep Blue (1997)
AlphaGo (2016)

Chess

blocks.text: DeepMind, the company behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold, is based in **London**. The UK has a long history in AI, from Turing onwards.

items: Alan Turing proposed the Turing test in 1950.
The term "artificial intelligence" dates from the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.
Deep Blue beat chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997.
AlphaGo beat Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016, using machine learning.
AI chatbots became widely used from late 2022.

practice.q: Describe how the **Turing test** works.
practice.a: A human judge has (typed) conversations with a hidden person and a hidden computer (1); the judge asks questions and must decide which is the computer (1); if the judge cannot reliably tell them apart, the computer passes (1).

practice.a: Any one: a program can fool people without understanding anything (1); modern chatbots can pass short conversations but still make basic mistakes (1); it only tests conversation, not other kinds of intelligence (1).

pages.spec: Explain the difference between narrow AI and general AI
pages.summary: Narrow AI is very good at one specific task, like playing chess or recognising faces. General AI would be able to learn and do any intellectual task a human can. All AI that exists today is narrow AI; general AI does not exist yet.

diagram.title: Narrow AI vs general AI
diagram.caption: Which one do you use every day?

states.label: Narrow AI
points: Cannot switch to a different task
E.g. face unlock, spam filter, chess AI

states.label: General AI
points: Could do any task a human can
Would learn new tasks like a person
Only found in science fiction so far

blocks.text: Deep Blue could beat the best chess player in the world. But could it tie a shoelace, tell a joke or play noughts and crosses? No. It could only play chess. This is the key idea behind **narrow** and **general** AI.
Narrow AI

**[[Narrow AI]]** (also called *weak AI*) is designed to do **one specific task**, or a small set of related tasks. It can be extremely good at that task, often better than any human, but it cannot transfer its skill to something different.

items: A spam filter is brilliant at sorting emails, but cannot drive a car.
A sat nav finds the quickest route, but cannot recognise your face.
A chess AI beats grandmasters, but cannot answer a Geography question.

blocks.text: General AI

**[[General AI]]** (also called *artificial general intelligence* or *AGI*) would be a system that could learn and carry out **any** intellectual task a human can: switch from doing your Maths homework to writing a poem to planning a school trip, and genuinely understand all of it.

General AI **does not exist yet**. Experts strongly disagree about whether or when it might be built: some think it is decades away, some think it may never happen. Be cautious of headlines that claim it has arrived.

head: Narrow AI
General AI
rows: Does it exist?
Yes: all AI today
No, not yet
What can it do?
One task, or a small group of related tasks
Any intellectual task a human can do
Can it switch tasks?
No: a chess AI cannot drive a car
Yes: it would learn new tasks like a person
Examples
Face unlock, spam filters, sat navs, chess AI
Only in science fiction so far

blocks.text: Chatbots can talk about almost any subject, so they can *seem* general. But they are still narrow in an important way: they are trained to produce likely text. They do not reliably reason, plan or understand the world, and they cannot, by themselves, ride a bike or make you a cup of tea.

blocks.title: Worked example: narrow or general?
blocks.context: A school buys a new AI system that reads pupils' handwritten Maths answers and marks them. A teacher says: "This AI is so clever it could teach the whole Maths department!" Is she right?
steps: The system does one job: recognising handwriting and checking answers. That is **narrow AI**.
Teaching needs many different skills: explaining, noticing when a pupil is upset, planning lessons, managing a class.
The marking AI cannot transfer its skill to any of these.
blocks.answer: No: it is narrow AI. It is useful for one task, but it could not replace a teacher.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Narrow AI does one specific task very well.
All AI that exists today is narrow AI.
General AI would be able to do any intellectual task a human can.
General AI does not exist yet, and experts disagree about when, or if, it will.
Chatbots may seem general, but they are still narrow in important ways.

check.why: All AI today is narrow AI.

check.why: AGI stands for artificial general intelligence.

practice.a: All current AI is narrow, i.e. only good at specific tasks (1); general AI that can do any task a human can does not exist yet (1).

pages.spec: Identify where AI is used in everyday life and describe what it does in each case
pages.summary: You meet AI every day: recommendation systems suggest videos and songs, voice assistants turn speech into actions, face unlock recognises you, spam filters sort email and sat navs predict the quickest route. Each one learns patterns from data.

diagram.title: What does the AI do?
diagram.caption: Match each everyday AI to what it does.

blocks.text: Think about the first hour after you wake up. Did you check your phone? Watch a video? Ask a smart speaker for the weather? You have probably used AI several times before you even reach school.
AI you use every day

What the AI does
What data it learns from

Predicts what you will want to watch, listen to or buy next

Uses **[[Speech recognition|speech recognition]]** to turn your voice into text, works out what you want, then replies
Thousands of hours of recorded speech in different accents

blocks.caption: Everyday AI

blocks.text: Recommendation systems in more detail

Recommendation systems are probably the AI you meet most. They look for patterns like this: *people who watched the same videos as you also watched this one*. The more you use the app, the more data it has about you, and the more personal its suggestions become.

blocks.title: Worked example: why did it recommend that?
blocks.context: Caoimhe watches three videos about Gaelic football skills and one about a GAA final. The next day her home page is full of Gaelic football videos, including a channel she has never seen before.
steps: The app records what Caoimhe watched and for how long.
It finds other users with similar viewing histories.
Those users often watched the new channel too.
It predicts Caoimhe will probably like it, so it recommends it.
blocks.answer: The AI spotted a pattern between Caoimhe's viewing and other people's. It does not "know" she likes Gaelic football; it predicts it from data.

blocks.text: Recommendation systems are designed to keep you watching for as long as possible. That can be useful, but it can also mean you only see more and more of the same kind of thing. This is sometimes called a **filter bubble**. It is worth choosing to look outside it now and again.
AI behind the scenes

Some AI you never see directly. Banks use AI to spot unusual card payments that might be fraud. Hospitals are testing AI that helps doctors spot signs of disease in scans. Farmers use AI with cameras and drones to check crops. In each case, the AI is spotting patterns in data faster than a person could.
For an exam-style answer, give the **use** *and* say **what the AI does**: for example, "A spam filter uses AI to *predict whether an email is spam* and moves it to a junk folder."

blocks.title: Key points
items: Recommendation systems predict what you will want next from your history and other users'.
Voice assistants use speech recognition to turn speech into text and actions.
Face unlock uses facial recognition to match your face.
Spam filters predict whether each email is spam or not.
Sat navs predict journey times from traffic data.
All of these are narrow AI that learn patterns from data.

check.q: Which everyday AI predicts how long a journey will take?
check.why: It uses live and past traffic data.

practice.a: One mark for each correct use with what it does, e.g. video app recommends videos you might like (1); face unlock recognises your face to open the phone (1); voice assistant understands spoken questions (1); sat nav predicts quickest route (1); predictive text suggests the next word (1); spam filter sorts junk email (1).

pages.spec: Describe how machine learning works using training data, labels, patterns and testing
pages.summary: Machine learning is a way of building AI where the computer learns from examples instead of being given rules. It is trained on labelled data, finds patterns, builds a model, and is then tested on new data it has not seen to check how accurate it is.

diagram.title: How machine learning works
diagram.caption: Click each stage. If testing goes badly, go back and improve the data.

nodes.label: Collect data
nodes.detail: Gather thousands of examples, e.g. photos of cats and dogs.

nodes.label: Label it
nodes.detail: Each example is tagged with the right answer: cat or dog.

nodes.label: Train
nodes.detail: The computer finds patterns linking each photo to its label, producing a model.

nodes.label: Test
nodes.detail: Show the model new labelled photos it has never seen. How many does it get right?

nodes.label: Use
nodes.detail: If it is accurate enough, use it for real. If not, go back for more or better data.

blocks.text: How did you learn what a dog is? Nobody gave you a list of rules like *"four legs, fur, tail, barks"* (a cat has four legs, fur and a tail too!). You just saw lots of dogs, and people said "dog". Eventually you could recognise dogs you had never met. **Machine learning** works in a surprisingly similar way.
What is machine learning?

**[[Machine learning]]** is a type of AI where a computer **learns from examples** instead of following rules written by a programmer. It finds **[[patterns|Pattern]]** in data and uses them to make predictions about new data.
Why not just write the rules?
For some problems, writing rules is almost impossible. Try writing rules to spot spam:

blocks.title: A rule-based spam filter (the old way)
blocks.output: Catches a few obvious spam emails, but spammers simply write "FR3E M0NEY" and it fails. A programmer would need to write thousands of rules, forever.

blocks.text: A machine learning spam filter is shown millions of real emails and works out for itself which words, links, senders and patterns usually mean spam. When spammers change tactics, it can be **retrained** on new examples.
The machine learning process

items: **Collect data.** Gather lots of examples, e.g. thousands of photos or emails.
**Label the data.** Each example is given the correct answer, called a **[[Label|label]]**: *cat* or *dog*, *spam* or *not spam*.
**Train.** The computer studies the **[[Training data|training data]]** and finds patterns that link the examples to their labels. The result is a **[[Model|model]]**.
**Test.** The model is given **[[Testing data|testing data]]**: new labelled examples it has *never seen*. We compare its answers with the real labels to measure its **[[Accuracy|accuracy]]**.
**Use (and improve).** If it is accurate enough, it is used for real. If not, collect more or better data and train again.

blocks.text: The testing data must be **different** from the training data. If you test a model on the same examples it learned from, it is like giving pupils the exact exam questions the day before: a high score proves nothing about whether they really learned.
Features: what the computer looks at

The details a model uses to make its decision are called **[[features|Feature]]**. For an email, features might be the words used, the number of links, or whether the sender is in your contacts. For a photo, features could be shapes, edges, colours and textures.
Neural networks

Many modern AI systems use a **[[Neural network|neural network]]**: a type of model loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of simple connected units. During training, the strength of each connection is adjusted bit by bit until the network gives the right answers for the training examples. A neural network with many layers is called **[[Deep learning|deep learning]]**.
Remember the process as **C-L-T-T-U**: **C**ollect, **L**abel, **T**rain, **T**est, **U**se.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Machine learning = computers learning from examples, not hand-written rules.
Training data is labelled with the correct answers.
Training finds patterns and produces a model.
The model is tested on new data it has not seen, to measure accuracy.
Features are the details the model uses to decide.
Neural networks are models made of layers of connected units; many layers = deep learning.

check.q: What is a label in machine learning?
o: The correct answer attached to a training example
check.why: E.g. each photo is labelled cat or dog.

check.q: Why must testing data be different from training data?
o: To check the model works on examples it has never seen
It does not need to be different
check.why: Otherwise a high score proves nothing.

check.q: What is produced when a computer is trained on data?
check.why: The model is what makes predictions.

check.q: Which is the correct order?
check.why: Collect, Label, Train, Test, then Use.

practice.q: Describe the stages of training and testing a machine learning model.
practice.a: Collect lots of data/examples (1); label the data with the correct answers (1); train the model so it finds patterns in the training data (1); test it on new/unseen data and compare its answers with the labels to measure accuracy (1).

practice.q: Explain why machine learning is often better than writing rules for a spam filter.
practice.a: There are too many possible spam emails to write rules for / spammers change their wording to get round rules (1); machine learning finds patterns itself from many examples and can be retrained on new examples (1).

practice.q: What is meant by **training data**?
practice.a: The (labelled) examples a machine learning model learns patterns from (1).

pages.spec: Work through a classifier example and calculate a model's accuracy
pages.summary: A classifier is a model that sorts things into groups, such as cat or dog, or spam or not spam. We judge it by its accuracy: the percentage of test examples it gets right. Mistakes often come from training data that was too small or not varied enough.

diagram.title: Test yourself: cat/dog classifier
diagram.caption: Click a hidden cell to check the answer.
head: Question
Answer
rows: What are the two classes?
Cat and dog
Why keep 200 photos aside?
To test on photos the model has never seen
180 right out of 200: accuracy?
Why were night photos wrong?
Hardly any night photos in the training data

Best way to improve it?

blocks.text: Year 8 have been asked to help the school's Eco Club build an AI that sorts photos from the school wildlife camera into **cat** or **dog**. Let's follow it step by step.
What is a classifier?

A **[[Classifier|classifier]]** is a machine learning model that sorts each input into one of a fixed set of groups, called **classes**. A spam filter is a classifier with two classes (*spam*, *not spam*). The wildlife camera classifier has two classes too (*cat*, *dog*).

blocks.title: Worked example: training a cat/dog classifier
blocks.context: The Eco Club has 1,000 photos from the camera. 500 show cats and 500 show dogs.
steps: **Label:** pupils tag each photo as *cat* or *dog*.
**Split:** they keep 800 photos for training and put 200 aside for testing (so the model never sees them while learning).
**Train:** the model studies the 800 training photos. It finds features that tend to go with each label, e.g. ear shape, snout length, eye shape and size.
**Test:** the model is shown the 200 test photos and gives a prediction for each one.
**Check:** compare each prediction with the real label. It gets 180 right and 20 wrong.

blocks.text: Calculating accuracy
**Accuracy** is the percentage of test examples the model classified correctly:

head: Step
Calculation
rows: Number correct
Total number tested
Divide
Turn into a percentage
blocks.caption: Accuracy = correct ÷ total × 100

blocks.text: Accuracy is never a guarantee. A model that is 90% accurate will still get about **1 in every 10** examples wrong. For important decisions (like medicine), a human should check.
Why did it get some wrong?
The pupils looked at the 20 mistakes. They noticed a pattern:

items: Most wrong answers were photos taken **at night**, but nearly all the training photos were taken in daylight.
A small fluffy dog was called a *cat*: there were very few small, fluffy dogs in the training data.
One photo showed **a fox**. The model had only two classes, so it *had* to say cat or dog. It said dog.

blocks.text: A model can only learn from the data it is given. If a type of example is missing or rare in the training data, the model will be poor at it. This is the same problem that causes **bias**, which you will meet later.

blocks.title: Worked example: improving the model
blocks.context: How could the Eco Club make the classifier more accurate?
steps: Add more night-time photos to the training data.
Add more variety: different breeds, sizes, colours and angles.
Add a third class, *other animal*, so foxes and badgers are not forced into the wrong group.
Retrain, then test again on new photos it has never seen.
blocks.answer: More, and more varied, training data usually leads to a more accurate model.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A classifier sorts inputs into groups called classes.
Data is split into training data and testing data.
Accuracy = number correct ÷ number tested × 100.
Even an accurate model still makes mistakes.
More, and more varied, training data usually improves accuracy.

check.q: A classifier gets 45 out of 50 test photos right. What is its accuracy?
What is a classifier?
o: A model that sorts inputs into groups
check.why: E.g. cat or dog, spam or not spam.

check.q: The model gets most night-time photos wrong. What is the most likely reason?
o: There were very few night-time photos in the training data
Cats only come out in the day
Accuracy cannot be measured at night
check.why: A model is poor at things that are missing from its training data.

check.q: Which change is most likely to improve the classifier?
o: Test it on the training photos
check.why: More and more varied data usually helps.

practice.q: A spam filter is tested on 400 emails and classifies 380 correctly. Calculate its accuracy. Show your working.
A classifier trained to recognise dogs keeps getting photos of small, fluffy dogs wrong. Explain why this might happen and how to fix it.
practice.a: There were few/no small fluffy dogs in the training data (1) so the model did not learn their features/patterns (1); fix by adding more (labelled) photos of small fluffy dogs and retraining (1).

practice.q: Explain why a classifier that is 90% accurate should not be fully trusted.
practice.a: It will still get about 1 in 10 examples wrong (1); for important decisions a human should check the result (1).

pages.spec: Explain in simple terms how generative AI and large language models produce text
pages.summary: Generative AI creates new content such as text, images or music. A large language model is trained on huge amounts of text and writes by repeatedly predicting a likely next word. This makes it fluent, but it does not check facts or understand like a person.

diagram.title: How a chatbot writes, one word at a time
diagram.caption: The loop repeats until the answer is complete.

items.label: Read the text so far
items.detail: Your prompt plus every word the chatbot has already written.

items.label: Score every possible next word
items.detail: Patterns from training give each word a probability: tea is likely, giraffe is not.

items.label: Choose a likely word
items.detail: Pick one of the most likely words. A little randomness means answers vary each time.

items.label: Add it and go again
items.detail: The new word becomes part of the text, and the loop repeats.

blocks.text: The AI you have met so far mostly *sorts* or *predicts*: spam or not spam, cat or dog, which video next. **[[Generative AI|Generative AI]]** goes further: it **creates new content**.

head: Generative AI can make…
Example
rows: Text
A chatbot writes a story, an email or an explanation
Images
A picture created from a description, e.g. *"a dragon reading a book in Enniskillen castle"*
Audio and music
A song in a certain style, or a voice reading text aloud
Video
Short video clips made from a written description
Computer code
A program written from an instruction
blocks.caption: Types of generative AI

blocks.text: Large language models

AI chatbots are powered by a **[[Large language model|large language model]]** (**LLM**). It is *large* because it is a huge neural network trained on an enormous amount of text: books, websites, articles and more, far more than any human could read in many lifetimes.
At its heart, an LLM does something that sounds very simple: **it predicts the next word**.

blocks.title: Worked example: predicting the next word
blocks.context: You type: *"After school I went home and had my…"*
steps: The model looks at all the words so far.
From patterns in its training text, it gives each possible next word a probability: *tea* (high), *dinner* (high), *homework* (lower), *giraffe* (almost zero).
It picks a likely word, say *tea*, and adds it to the text.
It then repeats the whole process to predict the word after *tea*, and so on, one word at a time.
blocks.answer: By predicting one likely word after another, very quickly, it builds whole sentences and paragraphs.

blocks.text: Strictly, LLMs predict **tokens**, which are words or parts of words, but "next word" is a good way to picture it. Your phone's predictive text does a very small version of the same thing.
How chatbots are trained

items: **Pre-training:** the model reads huge amounts of text and learns to predict the next word. This is where it picks up grammar, facts and styles of writing.
**Fine-tuning:** people rate and correct its answers so that it becomes more helpful, follows instructions and avoids harmful replies.
**Your prompt:** when you type a **[[Prompt|prompt]]**, the model continues the conversation by predicting the most suitable reply.

blocks.text: What this means for you

head: What an LLM is good at
What an LLM does NOT do
rows: Language
Writes fluent, well-structured text in many styles
Does not understand meaning the way you do
Facts
Often repeats common facts correctly
Does not automatically check facts against a trusted source
Confidence
Always sounds confident
Does not reliably know when it is wrong
Up to date?
Knows a lot about what was in its training text
May not know about recent events unless it can search the web

blocks.text: Because an LLM predicts *likely* words, not *true* ones, it can produce answers that sound perfect but are completely wrong. You will learn more about this on the next page.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Generative AI creates new content: text, images, audio, video and code.
A large language model is trained on huge amounts of text.
It writes by repeatedly predicting a likely next word.
Fine-tuning with human feedback makes it more helpful.
It sounds fluent and confident, but does not check facts or truly understand.

check.q: What makes generative AI different from a spam filter?
check.why: A spam filter sorts; generative AI generates.

check.q: At its simplest, what does a large language model do?
o: Predicts the next word, again and again
check.why: It builds text one likely word at a time.

check.q: What is a prompt?
o: The instruction or question you give an AI tool
check.why: The model replies to your prompt.

check.q: Why can an LLM give a confident answer that is wrong?
o: It predicts likely words, not checked facts
check.why: Likely is not the same as true.

practice.q: Explain, in simple terms, how a large language model produces an answer.
practice.a: It has been trained on huge amounts of text (1); it predicts the most likely next word based on patterns (1); it adds that word and repeats the process to build sentences (1).

practice.q: Give **two** types of content that generative AI can create.
practice.a: Any two: text (1); images (1); music/audio/voices (1); video (1); computer code (1).

practice.q: Explain why predictive text on a phone is like a large language model.
practice.a: Both predict the next (likely) word (1) based on patterns learned from text (1).

pages.spec: Describe the limitations of AI, including hallucinations and bias in training data
pages.summary: AI can hallucinate: it can make up facts, quotes and sources that sound real. It can also be biased, because it learns from data that may be unbalanced or reflect unfair decisions from the past. AI output must always be checked.

diagram.title: Limitation or not?
diagram.caption: Match each situation to the problem it shows.
pairs: A chatbot invents a book that does not exist
Face recognition works worse for some skin tones
A job AI prefers men because past staff were men
A fake web link in an AI answer
Nobody can explain why the AI decided
A muffin is labelled as a dog

blocks.text: AI can be impressive, but it has real weaknesses. Knowing them is what makes you a smart user rather than a fooled one.
Hallucinations

A **[[Hallucination|hallucination]]** is when an AI tool produces information that is **false or made up**, but presents it as though it were true. Remember: an LLM predicts *likely-sounding* words. If it does not have the right information, it may still produce something that *sounds* right.

blocks.title: Worked example: the made-up book
blocks.context: Oisín asks a chatbot for three books about the history of Enniskillen, with authors, for his History homework.
steps: The chatbot gives three titles with authors and dates. They look completely believable.
Oisín searches the library catalogue and the internet for each one.
One is real. The other two do not exist: the chatbot invented titles that *sound* like real local history books.
blocks.answer: This is a hallucination. Oisín was right to check before putting them in his bibliography.

items: AI can invent facts, dates, quotes, statistics, web links and references.
It can get Maths wrong while showing confident-looking working.
It may not know about recent events.
It rarely says "I don't know" unless it has been designed to.

blocks.text: **Never** copy facts, quotes or references from an AI tool into your work without checking them in a reliable source.
Bias

**[[Bias|Bias]]** in AI is when a system gives results that are **unfair** to certain groups of people. AI is not biased on purpose. It learns patterns from its training data, so **if the data is unbalanced or unfair, the AI will be too**. People sometimes sum this up as *"bias in, bias out"*.

head: Example
What happened
Why
rows: Recruitment AI

In 2018 it was reported that a large tech company had scrapped an experimental AI for sorting job applications, because it marked down CVs that included the word "women's" (as in "women's chess club").
It had learned from ten years of past CVs, most of which came from men, so it learned to prefer male applicants.
Facial recognition
A 2018 study (*Gender Shades*, by researcher Joy Buolamwini) found that some commercial face-analysis systems were far less accurate for darker-skinned women than for lighter-skinned men.
The training photos contained far more lighter-skinned faces, especially men's.
Image generators
When asked for a picture of "a doctor" or "a CEO", some image generators have mostly shown men, and for "a nurse" mostly women.
The images they learned from reflected stereotypes.
blocks.caption: Real examples of AI bias

blocks.title: Worked example: spot the bias
blocks.context: A school builds an AI to recommend which pupils should be invited to an advanced Maths club. It is trained on records of who joined the club over the last 20 years. In the past, mostly boys were invited.
steps: The training data shows mostly boys in the club.
The AI learns the pattern *"club members are usually boys"*.
It is likely to recommend more boys than girls, even when girls have equal or better Maths results.
blocks.answer: The AI has copied past unfairness from its data. To reduce bias, use balanced data, base the decision on the right features (like Maths results), test the results for each group, and keep a teacher in charge of the final decision.

blocks.text: Other limitations

items: **No common sense:** AI can make mistakes no person would make, e.g. labelling a picture of a muffin as a dog.
**Black box:** with large neural networks it is often hard to explain *why* the AI made a decision.
**Energy and water:** training and running large AI models uses a lot of electricity in data centres, and water to cool them.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A hallucination is when AI makes up false information that sounds real.
Always check AI facts, quotes and references in a reliable source.
Bias means AI treats some groups unfairly.
Bias usually comes from unbalanced or unfair training data: bias in, bias out.
Reduce bias with balanced data, testing on different groups and human oversight.

check.q: What is an AI hallucination?
o: When AI makes up false information that sounds true
check.why: It sounds confident but is wrong.

check.q: Where does bias in AI usually come from?
check.why: Bias in, bias out.

check.q: A chatbot gives you a quote from a famous scientist for your project. What should you do?
o: Check it in a reliable source first
Ask the chatbot if it is sure, then use it
check.why: The chatbot could have made it up; asking it again is not real checking.

check.q: Which is the best way to reduce bias in an AI system?
o: Train it on more balanced data and test results for different groups
Let it make all decisions on its own
check.why: Balanced data, testing and human oversight all help.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **bias** in AI and how it can happen.
practice.a: Bias is when an AI gives results that are unfair to certain groups (1); AI learns patterns from its training data (1); if the data is unbalanced/reflects past unfairness, the AI copies it (1).

practice.q: Describe **one** real example of AI bias.
practice.a: e.g. recruitment AI trained on mostly men's CVs (1) marked down CVs mentioning women (1). OR: facial recognition trained mostly on lighter-skinned faces (1) was less accurate for darker-skinned women (1). OR: image generators (1) showing stereotypes such as doctors as men (1).

practice.q: A pupil uses a chatbot to find statistics for a Geography project. Give **two** pieces of advice.
practice.a: Any two: the chatbot may hallucinate/make up figures (1); check each statistic in a reliable source, e.g. a government or official website (1); record the real source, not the chatbot (1); be aware the data may be out of date (1).

pages.spec: Discuss ethical issues in AI, including honesty in schoolwork, privacy, deepfakes and jobs
pages.summary: Using AI raises ethical questions. Passing off AI work as your own is cheating; personal data you type in may be stored; deepfakes can spread lies and hurt people; and AI will change many jobs, removing some tasks and creating new ones.

diagram.title: Test yourself: right or wrong?
diagram.caption: Decide, then click a hidden cell to check.
head: Situation
Verdict
rows: Ask AI to quiz you on French vocabulary
Fine: it helps you learn
Hand in an AI-written story as your own
Plagiarism: dishonest
Upload a friend's photo to an AI app without asking
Wrong: it breaks their privacy
Make a fake video of a teacher for a laugh
Harmful deepfake: could be bullying
Use AI to brainstorm ideas, then tell your teacher you used it
Usually fine, if your teacher allows it
Type your school password into a chatbot
Never: keep personal data private

blocks.text: Just because AI *can* do something does not mean it *should*. **[[Ethics]]** is about deciding what is right and wrong. With AI, there are big ethical questions that affect you directly.
Honesty in schoolwork

Handing in work written by AI as if it were your own is a form of **[[Plagiarism|plagiarism]]**: presenting someone else's work as yours. It is dishonest, and it also means *you* don't learn, which shows up in exams where there is no AI to help.

head: Using AI to help you learn
Using AI to cheat
rows: Example
Asking it to explain photosynthesis a different way, then writing notes in your own words
Asking it to write your English essay, then handing it in
Who does the thinking?
You
The AI
Honest?
Yes, if your teacher allows it and you say you used it
No: it is plagiarism
Result in exams
You understand the topic
You are stuck, because you never learned it

blocks.text: For GCSE and A-level coursework, exam boards treat submitting AI-generated work as your own as **malpractice**. Penalties can include losing marks or being disqualified. Always follow your teacher's and school's rules on AI.
Privacy
Many AI tools store what you type, and some use it to train future models. Protect your **[[Personal data|personal data]]**:

items: Never type your full name, address, phone number, passwords or school login into an AI chatbot.
Don't upload photos of friends or family without their permission.
Don't share other people's private information, including friends' messages.
Many AI tools have a minimum age (often 13, sometimes 18). Check the rules and use only tools your school or parents allow.

blocks.text: Deepfakes

A **[[Deepfake|deepfake]]** is a fake image, video or audio clip, made using AI, that shows a real person saying or doing something they never said or did. Some are made as obvious jokes, but deepfakes can be used to:

items: spread false news, e.g. a fake video of a politician before an election;
scam people, e.g. a cloned voice of a family member asking for money;
bully or humiliate someone, e.g. a fake embarrassing image of a classmate.

blocks.title: Worked example: what should Ellie do?
blocks.context: Ellie sees a fake, embarrassing image of a girl in her year being shared in a group chat. Someone says it was "just made with an AI app for a laugh".
steps: It is not a joke: it is harmful to the girl, and making or sharing it is a form of **cyberbullying**.
Making or sharing a fake sexual image of anyone under 18 is a serious crime, even if it was made with an AI app.
Ellie should not share it or react to it, should keep evidence if she can do so safely, and tell a trusted adult.
blocks.answer: Don't share, tell a trusted adult. Deepfakes of real people can cause serious harm.

blocks.text: To spot a possible deepfake: look for odd details (hands, teeth, earrings, blurred edges, strange lighting), check whether trusted news sources are reporting it, and ask: *who posted this, and why?*
Jobs

AI will change many jobs. Some tasks, such as sorting documents or answering simple customer questions, are already being done by AI. But history shows that new technology also **creates** jobs: people are needed to build, test, check and manage AI systems. Many jobs will change rather than disappear, with people using AI as a tool. Skills like creativity, teamwork, caring for others and good judgement remain very valuable.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Ethics is about what is right and wrong.
Passing off AI work as your own is plagiarism, and in coursework it is malpractice.
Never type personal data into AI tools; check age limits.
Deepfakes are AI-made fakes of real people; they can spread lies, scam and bully.
AI will replace some tasks, change many jobs and create new ones.

check.q: Which is an honest use of AI for homework (if your teacher allows it)?
o: Copying an AI essay and handing it in
Asking AI to explain a topic, then writing it in your own words
Getting AI to do your test
Changing a few words in an AI essay so it looks like yours
check.why: You do the thinking and the writing.

check.q: What is a deepfake?
o: An AI-made fake image, video or audio of a real person
check.why: It shows someone saying or doing something they never did.

check.q: Which should you NEVER type into an AI chatbot?
check.why: Protect your personal data.

check.q: What is the most likely effect of AI on jobs?
o: Some tasks will be automated, many jobs will change and new jobs will be created
check.why: A balanced view: change, not simply loss.

practice.q: Explain why handing in AI-generated work as your own is wrong.
practice.a: It is dishonest/plagiarism, as you are claiming work that is not yours (1); you don't learn the topic, so you struggle in exams / it can be malpractice with penalties (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** ways deepfakes can cause harm.
practice.a: Any two: spreading false news/misinformation (1); scams, e.g. cloned voices asking for money (1); bullying or humiliating someone (1); damaging someone's reputation (1).

practice.q: Discuss how AI might affect jobs in the future. Give a balanced answer.
practice.a: Some tasks/jobs may be done by AI, e.g. simple customer service or sorting documents (1); new jobs will be created building, testing or managing AI (1); many jobs will change, with people using AI as a tool / human skills like creativity and care stay valuable (1).

pages.spec: Use AI tools well by writing clear prompts, checking facts and citing AI use
pages.summary: To use AI tools well, write clear prompts that give context, a task and a format; check every fact in a reliable source; and be honest by saying when and how you used AI. AI should support your thinking, not replace it.

diagram.title: Using AI well
diagram.caption: A good habit to follow every time.

items.label: Prompt
items.detail: Give context, a clear task, a format and limits.

items.label: Read critically
items.detail: Does it make sense? Is it at the right level?

items.label: Check
items.detail: Confirm facts, quotes and links in reliable sources.

items.label: Refine
items.detail: Ask a better follow-up question if the answer wasn't right.

items.label: Write and cite
items.detail: Put it in your own words and say how you used AI.

blocks.text: Used well, AI can be a brilliant study partner: it can explain things in a new way, quiz you and help you plan. Used badly, it gives you wrong answers that you don't notice. The difference is **how** you use it.
Writing good prompts
A good **prompt** gives the AI enough information to give you a useful answer. Try including:

head: Part of the prompt
What it means
Example
rows: **Role or context**
Who you are and what you need it for
"I'm a Year 9 pupil in Northern Ireland revising for a Geography test."
**Task**
Exactly what you want it to do
"Explain how a volcano forms."
**Format**
How you want the answer laid out
"Use 5 bullet points with simple words."
**Limits**
Length, level or things to avoid
"Keep it under 100 words."
blocks.caption: The parts of a good prompt

blocks.title: Worked example: improving a prompt
blocks.context: Niall types: *"volcanoes"*. He gets a long, complicated essay he can't use.
steps: Add context: *"I'm in Year 9 revising for a Geography test."*
Add a clear task: *"Explain how a volcano forms and why some erupt explosively."*
Add a format: *"Use 5 short bullet points."*
Ask it to help him learn: *"Then give me 3 quiz questions to test myself, without the answers."*
blocks.answer: The improved prompt gets a short, useful answer at the right level, plus a quick self-test.

blocks.text: If the first answer isn't right, don't give up: **refine** your prompt. Ask for it to be simpler, shorter, or to give an example.
Checking facts
Remember hallucinations. Before you use anything an AI tool tells you:

items: **Check** important facts, dates, figures and quotes in at least one reliable source, such as a textbook, your class notes, BBC Bitesize or an official website.
**Look for real sources.** If the AI gives a link or book, open it or find it yourself to make sure it exists and says what the AI claims.
**Ask yourself:** does this make sense with what I already know?
**Ask a teacher** if two sources disagree.

blocks.text: Citing AI use
Being honest about AI use is part of good **[[Citation|citation]]**: saying where information came from. If your teacher allows AI for a task, record:

items: the AI tool you used (a general description is fine, e.g. "an AI chatbot" plus its name);
the date you used it;
the prompt(s) you typed;
what you used it for, e.g. "to help plan my essay" or "to explain a topic".

blocks.title: Worked example: an AI acknowledgement
blocks.context: Saoirse used an AI chatbot to help plan her ICT project on renewable energy, with her teacher's permission.
steps: She keeps a copy of her prompts and the replies.
She checks every fact she uses in reliable sources and cites *those* sources in her bibliography.
At the end she adds a note.
blocks.answer: *"I used an AI chatbot on 12 March to suggest headings for my project plan. Prompt: 'Suggest five headings for a Year 10 project on renewable energy in Northern Ireland.' All facts were checked and are referenced from the sources listed."*

blocks.text: Think of AI as a **study partner**, not a ghostwriter. If you could not explain your work to your teacher without the AI, you have let it do too much.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A good prompt gives context, a clear task, a format and limits.
Refine your prompt if the first answer is not useful.
Check every important fact in a reliable source.
Record the tool, date, prompts and what you used AI for.
Use AI to support your learning, not to replace your thinking.

check.q: Which is the best prompt?
o: I'm in Year 9. Explain how volcanoes form in 5 short bullet points.
check.why: It gives context, a task and a format.

check.q: An AI tool gives you a website link as a source. What should you do?
o: Copy it straight into your bibliography
Open it to check it exists and says what the AI claims
Ask the AI to promise it is real
check.why: AI can hallucinate links.

check.q: Which of these should you record when citing AI use?
o: The tool, the date and the prompts you used
check.why: This shows honestly how you used it.

check.q: What should you do if the AI's first answer is too complicated?
o: Refine the prompt, e.g. ask for simpler words
check.why: Refining prompts gets better answers.

practice.q: Rewrite the prompt *"tell me about Northern Ireland"* to make it more useful for a Year 8 History homework. Explain **two** improvements you made.
practice.a: Improved prompt including at least context and a clear task (1), e.g. "I'm in Year 8 doing History homework. Explain three reasons why the Giant's Causeway is important, in simple bullet points." Explanation: added context so the answer is at the right level (1); added a specific task/format/length so the answer is focused and usable (1).

practice.q: Explain **two** ways to check whether information from an AI chatbot is accurate.
practice.a: Any two: check it against a reliable source, e.g. textbook/BBC Bitesize/official website (1); open any links/find any books to make sure they exist (1); compare with what you already know/class notes (1); ask a teacher (1).

practice.q: State **three** things a pupil should record when acknowledging AI use in a piece of work.
practice.a: Any three: the AI tool used (1); the date (1); the prompts typed (1); what it was used for / which part of the work (1).

glossary.def: Computer systems that can do tasks that would normally need human intelligence, such as recognising faces, understanding speech or making predictions.
A set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task.
Facts, figures, text, images or sounds that a computer can store and process.
A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 in which a judge has typed conversations with a hidden person and a hidden computer and tries to tell which is the computer.
A program that holds a conversation with a person using text or speech.
AI designed to do one specific task, or a small set of related tasks, very well. All AI today is narrow AI.
A possible future AI that could learn and do any intellectual task a human can. It does not exist yet.
AI that predicts what a user will want next (a video, song or product) from their history and that of similar users.
AI software that listens to spoken requests and carries them out, often on a phone or smart speaker.
Technology that turns spoken words into text a computer can use.
AI that identifies or checks a person from an image of their face, e.g. face unlock.
AI that predicts whether an email is junk (spam) and moves it out of the inbox.
A type of AI in which a computer learns patterns from examples (data) instead of following rules written by a programmer.
Something that repeats or links examples together, which a machine learning model can learn and use to make predictions.
The correct answer attached to a training example, e.g. cat or dog, spam or not spam.
The labelled examples a machine learning model learns from.
What machine learning produces after training: the learned patterns used to make predictions about new data.
New labelled examples, not used in training, that are used to check how accurate a model is.
The percentage of test examples a model gets right: number correct ÷ number tested × 100.
A detail or measurable property the model uses to make a decision, e.g. the words in an email or the shape of an ear in a photo.
A type of machine learning model loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of simple connected units.
Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers.
A machine learning model that sorts each input into one of a set of groups (classes), e.g. spam or not spam.
AI that creates new content, such as text, images, music, video or code.
A very large neural network trained on huge amounts of text that writes by repeatedly predicting a likely next word. It powers AI chatbots.
The instruction or question you give to an AI tool.
When an AI tool produces false or made-up information but presents it as true.
When an AI system gives results that are unfair to certain groups of people, usually because of unbalanced or unfair training data.
Deciding what is morally right and wrong, e.g. whether and how AI should be used.
Presenting someone else's work (including work written by AI) as your own.
Information that identifies you, such as your name, address, phone number, photos or passwords.
A fake image, video or audio clip made with AI that shows a real person saying or doing something they never said or did.
A note saying where information came from, including when and how an AI tool was used.
